title: The Liberty of Thought
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from On Liberty by John Stuart Mill (1859).
body: Apart from the peculiar tenets of individual thinkers, there is also in the world at large an increasing inclination to stretch unduly the powers of society over the individual, both by the force of opinion and even by that of legislation: and as the tendency of all the changes taking place in the world is to strengthen society, and diminish the power of the individual, this encroachment is not one of the evils which tend spontaneously to disappear, but, on the contrary, to grow more and more formidable. The disposition of mankind, whether as rulers or as fellow-citizens to impose their own opinions and inclinations as a rule of conduct on others, is so energetically supported by some of the best and by some of the worst feelings incident to human nature, that it is hardly ever kept under restraint by anything but want of power; and as the power is not declining, but growing, unless a strong barrier of moral conviction can be raised against the mischief, we must expect, in the present circumstances of the world, to see it increase.

It will be convenient for the argument, if, instead of at once entering upon the general thesis, we confine ourselves in the first instance to a single branch of it, on which the principle here stated is, if not fully, yet to a certain point, recognised by the current opinions. This one branch is the Liberty of Thought: from which it is impossible to separate the cognate liberty of speaking and of writing.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, through what two means does society's power over the individual increase?
options: The force of opinion and legislation
Wealth and military strength
Religion and education alone
Fear and violence

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what does the author say is "hardly ever kept under restraint by anything but want of power"?
options: Mankind's disposition to impose their own opinions on others
The growth of legislation
The spread of new inventions
The rise of individual thinkers

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what single branch does the author choose to focus on first?
options: The Liberty of Thought
The Liberty of Trade
The Liberty of Assembly
The Liberty of Religion

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what two liberties does the author say are inseparable from the Liberty of Thought?
options: The liberty of speaking and of writing
The liberty of travel and trade
The liberty of voting and assembly
The liberty of worship and silence

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author say the encroachment of society on the individual is not an evil that will "spontaneously disappear"?
options: The general trend of change in the world is to strengthen society and weaken the individual, not the reverse
Governments have passed laws specifically protecting the encroachment
Most individuals actively support the loss of their own liberty
No one has ever tried to resist this encroachment before

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author say the desire to impose one's opinions on others is supported by both "the best and the worst feelings" in human nature?
options: Such impositions can come from sincere moral conviction as well as from selfish or domineering impulses
Only evil people ever try to impose their opinions on others
Good feelings and bad feelings are actually the same thing
The author believes imposing opinions is always justified

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author believe a "strong barrier of moral conviction" is necessary against this trend?
options: Growing social power isn't naturally checked by anything except a lack of power, so only firm moral principle can hold it back
Legislation alone is always sufficient to stop such trends
Moral conviction was already strong enough in the author's time
The trend was expected to reverse on its own

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author choose to begin with a single branch of the argument rather than the whole thesis at once?
options: That branch is already recognized to some degree by current opinion, making it a more convenient starting point
The author had no time to address the whole thesis
The whole thesis was considered too controversial to state directly
Readers had specifically requested this branch be discussed first

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the overall point of the passage?
options: Society's power over individuals tends to grow unchecked unless resisted by firm moral conviction, and the author will begin examining this through the liberty of thought
Society's power over individuals is declining rapidly and needs no resistance
Individual liberty was fully protected in the author's time
Legislation is the only threat to individual liberty

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean that this encroachment tends to grow "more formidable"?
options: More powerful and difficult to resist
More rare and unlikely to occur
More popular among ordinary citizens
More easily reversed over time

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the author say is the general tendency of changes taking place in the world?
options: To strengthen society and diminish the power of the individual
To weaken all forms of government
To increase individual liberty at every turn
To eliminate the need for moral conviction

questions.prompt: Per the passage, who does the author say has a disposition to impose their opinions on others as a rule of conduct?
options: Mankind, whether as rulers or as fellow-citizens
Only kings and emperors
Only religious leaders
Only professional philosophers

questions.prompt: According to the passage, is the power to impose opinions on others declining or growing?
options: Growing
Declining
Staying exactly the same
Unknown, according to the author

questions.prompt: Per the passage, to what extent is the principle behind the Liberty of Thought already recognized by current opinion?
options: To a certain point, though not fully
Completely and universally
Not at all
Only among a small circle of philosophers

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author call the liberty of speaking and writing "cognate" to the liberty of thought?
options: They are so closely related that they cannot be meaningfully separated from one another
They developed in entirely different historical periods
They are opposites that constantly conflict with each other
They apply only to professional writers and speakers

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes why the author starts with the Liberty of Thought?
options: It offers the clearest, most widely accepted starting point for a broader argument about individual liberty
It is the least important of all the liberties discussed
It has nothing to do with the rest of the argument
It was the only liberty the author personally valued

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean to "stretch unduly" the powers of society over the individual?
options: To extend those powers beyond what is proper or justified
To reduce those powers to almost nothing
To apply those powers only in emergencies
To transfer those powers to a foreign government
